title: The Price of a Falling Rupee
problem: Between 2015 and 2025, food prices in Pakistan nearly tripled. Over the same period the rupee lost much of its value against the US dollar, while world food prices rose only a little. We want to know whether the weak rupee is driving food inflation.
question: Does a weaker rupee, along with world food prices and fuel costs, raise food inflation in Pakistan — and does a stronger rupee bring it down?

variables.name: Food Inflation
variables.measure: Monthly % change in Pakistan's national food price index
variables.why: How fast food prices rise each month — what we want to explain.

variables.name: Rupee Depreciation
variables.measure: Monthly % change in rupees per US dollar (last month)
variables.why: A positive number = the rupee got weaker, so imports cost more.

variables.name: World Food Inflation
variables.measure: Monthly % change in the FAO Food Price Index (last month)
variables.why: How fast world prices of wheat, oil, sugar, dairy and meat are rising.

variables.name: Fuel & Transport Inflation
variables.measure: Monthly % change in the transport price index (last month)
variables.why: Fuel is needed to grow food and move it to the market.

variables.name: Last Month's Food Inflation
variables.why: Price rises tend to continue — this captures that momentum.

equation_general: Food Inflation = β₀ + β₁ Rupee Depreciation + β₂ World Food Inflation + β₃ Fuel & Transport Inflation + β₄ Last Month's Food Inflation + error
equation_estimated: Food Inflation = 0.50 + 0.27 Rupee Depreciation + 0.12 World Food Inflation − 0.05 Fuel & Transport Inflation + 0.18 Last Month's Food Inflation
equation_note: All variables are monthly % changes. The X variables are measured one month earlier, because prices take time to react. Estimated by ordinary least squares (OLS) on 132 months, January 2015 – December 2025.

coefficients.name: Rupee Depreciation (last month)
coefficients.plain: If the rupee falls 1% this month, food prices rise about 0.27% next month (a 10% fall → about 2.7%).

coefficients.name: World Food Inflation (last month)
coefficients.plain: Positive (0.12) but not significant (p = 0.12): month to month, world prices do not clearly pass into Pakistan's food prices.

coefficients.name: Fuel & Transport Inflation (last month)
coefficients.plain: Close to zero (-0.05) and not significant (p = 0.43): no clear month-to-month effect.

coefficients.name: Food Inflation (last month)
coefficients.plain: Food inflation carries over: 18% of last month's rise repeats this month.

hypotheses.question: Does a weaker rupee raise food inflation?
Does world food inflation raise Pakistan's food inflation?
hypotheses.h0: World food inflation has no effect (β₂ = 0).

hypotheses.question: Does fuel & transport inflation raise food inflation?
hypotheses.h0: Fuel & transport inflation has no effect (β₃ = 0).

hypotheses.question: Does food inflation carry over from last month? (autoregression)
hypotheses.h0: Last month's food inflation has no effect (β₄ = 0).

hypotheses.question: Do the variables together explain food inflation?
hypotheses.h0: All slopes are zero (β₁ = β₂ = β₃ = β₄ = 0).
hypotheses.h1: At least one slope is not zero.

hypotheses.question: Does a rising rupee affect food prices as much as a falling rupee?
hypotheses.h0: Depreciation and appreciation have the same effect.
hypotheses.result: Falling rupee 0.33 (p = 0.004); rising rupee -0.00 (p = 0.988); F = 1.35, p = 0.247

tests.name: Descriptive Statistics
tests.checks: Average, spread, lowest and highest value of each variable.
tests.result: Food prices +194%, dollar rate +178%, world food +23% (2015→2025).
tests.meaning: Pakistan's food prices rose far more than world food prices.

tests.name: Correlation
tests.checks: How strongly two variables move together (−1 to +1).
tests.result: Levels: food vs dollar r = 0.98. Monthly changes: food inflation vs last month's depreciation r = 0.23.
tests.meaning: Levels move together almost perfectly; month-to-month links are weaker but positive.

tests.name: Stationarity (ADF Unit Root Test)
tests.checks: Whether a series has a stable average or keeps trending.
tests.h0: The series is non-stationary (has a unit root).
tests.result: Levels: all p > 0.05 (non-stationary). Monthly % changes: all p < 0.001 (stationary).
tests.meaning: Regressing trending levels can give fake results, so the model uses monthly % changes, which are stationary.

tests.name: Multicollinearity (VIF)
tests.checks: Whether the independent variables are too similar to each other.
tests.meaning: Each variable brings its own information, so the coefficients are reliable.

tests.name: Regression (OLS, t-tests)
tests.checks: How much each variable moves food inflation, and whether the effect is significant.
tests.result: Rupee depreciation p = 0.007; last month's food inflation p = 0.040; world food p = 0.122; fuel p = 0.428.
tests.meaning: A weaker rupee and last month's food inflation significantly raise food inflation.

tests.name: Overall Significance (F-test) & R²
tests.checks: Whether the model as a whole explains food inflation.
tests.meaning: The model is significant. It explains about 10% of monthly ups and downs — normal for monthly food prices, which also jump with weather and harvests.

tests.name: Autocorrelation (Durbin-Watson & Breusch-Godfrey)
tests.checks: Whether errors from one month repeat in the next.
tests.result: DW = 2.04 (≈ 2 is ideal); BG(12 lags) p = 0.207
tests.meaning: No autocorrelation — the errors are independent. (BG is the main test because the model has a lagged Y.)

tests.name: Heteroskedasticity (Breusch-Pagan & White)
tests.checks: Whether the size of the errors changes with the variables.
tests.meaning: No heteroskedasticity — error size is stable, so the p-values can be trusted.

tests.name: Normality (Jarque-Bera)
tests.checks: Whether the errors follow a normal (bell-shaped) distribution.
tests.meaning: The errors are normal enough — t- and F-tests are valid.

tests.name: Specification (Ramsey RESET)
tests.checks: Whether the equation's form is correct (nothing important missing).

tests.name: Asymmetry (Wald F-test)
tests.checks: Whether a falling and a rising rupee have the same effect.
tests.result: Falling rupee 0.33 (p = 0.004); rising rupee -0.00 (p = 0.988); test p = 0.247
tests.meaning: A falling rupee clearly raises food prices; a rising rupee shows no effect — but the difference is not statistically proven.

answer: YES — a weaker rupee raises food inflation. A 1% fall in the rupee adds about 0.27% to food prices the next month (about 0.33% in total once the carry-over is included). Significant at 1% (p = 0.007).
Food inflation has momentum: about 18% of last month's rise carries into this month (p = 0.040).
NO clear month-to-month effect of world food prices (p = 0.122) or fuel & transport costs (p = 0.428).
A rising rupee showed no effect on food prices (-0.00, p = 0.988), while a falling rupee did (0.33, p = 0.004) — but the difference is not statistically proven (p = 0.247).
The model passes all diagnostic tests: no multicollinearity, no autocorrelation, no heteroskedasticity, normal errors, correct form.
one_line: When the rupee falls, food prices follow a month later — and nothing in our data shows them coming back down when the rupee recovers.
